```plato

    //==
    // # Derived row access over the IJagged interface
    //
    // Row arithmetic written once against `IJagged<T>`
    // (`collections.concepts.plato`) so no mesh or adjacency file re-derives
    // offset slicing. Interface-receiver form throughout, as in the sections above.
    //
    // `JaggedArray<T>` needs no projection here: its `Offsets` and `Values` fields
    // satisfy the interface surface directly, so a type that HOLDS one reaches the row
    // vocabulary through that field (`mesh.Faces.Row(f)`). The projections for the
    // domain types that implement IJagged over differently-named storage live beside
    // those types (`topology.library.plato`).

    //==
    // # IJagged<T>
    //
    // Accessors derived from the two obligations. Every row query is bounds-free
    // by construction: the caller supplies a row in [0, RowCount).

    // The number of rows: one fewer than the number of offset boundaries.
    RowCount(self: IJagged<$T>): Integer
        => self.Offsets.Count - 1;

    // The number of items in row i: Offsets[i+1] - Offsets[i].
    // Precondition: 0 <= i < RowCount.
    RowLength(self: IJagged<$T>, i: Integer): Integer
        => self.Offsets[i + 1] - self.Offsets[i];

    // The items of row i, copied out of the packed Values array.
    // Precondition: 0 <= i < RowCount.
    Row(self: IJagged<$T>, i: Integer): Array<$T>
        => self.Values.SubArray(self.Offsets[i], self.RowLength(i));

    // The k-th item of row `row`, addressed without materializing the row.
    // Precondition: 0 <= row < RowCount and 0 <= k < RowLength(row).
    RowElement(self: IJagged<$T>, row: Integer, k: Integer): $T
        => self.Values[self.Offsets[row] + k];

    // True when there are no rows at all (the empty encoding: Offsets = [0]).
    HasNoRows(self: IJagged<$T>): Boolean
        => self.RowCount.IsZero;

    //==
    // # Builders
    //
    // A plain library function rather than an interface member: static-abstract
    // interface members are not available in this language yet.

    // Pack an array of rows into a JaggedArray: Offsets is the exclusive prefix
    // sum of the row lengths (hence Count + 1 entries, last equal to the total),
    // Values is the rows flattened in order.
    // C# oracle: `Ara3D.Geometry.Primitives.PolygonMesh3D`.
    // The fold runs over integer row LENGTHS rather than over the rows: a lambda
    // parameter that is itself a collection binds Count ambiguously (Array vs the
    // unique List builder), which the checker rejects.
    FromRows(rows: Array<Array<$T>>): JaggedArray<$T>
    {
        var offsets = (rows.Count + 1).MapRange(i => i.MapRange(j => rows[j].Count).Reduce(0, (acc, n) => acc + n));
        return (offsets, rows.FlatMap(r => r));
    }

    //==
    // # Collections sampling
    //
    // The array-producing primitives under every "evaluate this thing at n evenly
    // spaced parameters" helper: evenly spaced fractions of the unit interval and
    // their interpolated counterparts
    // (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_interpolation).

    //==
    // # Sampling and discretization
    //
    // The array-producing primitive under every "evaluate this thing at n evenly
    // spaced parameters" helper: curve Sample / ToPolyline, CirclePoints,
    // RegularPolygon vertices, and grid tessellation. These live in this package
    // (P2) rather than with IInterpolatable (P1) because they are fundamentally
    // collection *construction*: no interface in this tree can build a collection,
    // so they are written directly against the `Integer.Range` and `Array.Map`
    // intrinsics. P1 may not call P2, hence the LinearSpace-over-IInterpolatable
    // overloads live here too rather than in core-algebra.

    // `count` evenly spaced parameters spanning the closed unit interval:
    // element i is i / (count - 1), so the first is 0 and the last is exactly 1.
    // Precondition: count >= 2. This is the right form for an OPEN curve, where
    // both endpoints are wanted.
    Fractions(count: Integer): Array<Number>
        => count.Range.Map(i => i.ToNumber / (count - 1).ToNumber);

    // `count` evenly spaced parameters spanning the half-open unit interval:
    // element i is i / count, so the first is 0 and 1 is never reached.
    // Precondition: count >= 1. This is the right form for a CLOSED (periodic)
    // curve, where parameter 1 would duplicate parameter 0.
    FractionsExclusive(count: Integer): Array<Number>
        => count.Range.Map(i => i.ToNumber / count.ToNumber);

    // `count` evenly spaced parameters over [0, 1], endpoints included. The
    // numpy-style spelling of Fractions; both names are kept because callers read
    // "linear space" for sampling and "fractions" for index arithmetic.
    LinearSpace(count: Integer): Array<Number>
        => count.Fractions;

    // `count` evenly spaced parameters over [0, 1), the upper end excluded.
    LinearSpaceExclusive(count: Integer): Array<Number>
        => count.FractionsExclusive;

    // `count` evenly spaced values from a to b inclusive, for anything that can be
    // interpolated (numbers, points, vectors, colors, transforms).
    // Precondition: count >= 2.
    LinearSpace(a: IInterpolatable, b: IInterpolatable, count: Integer): Array<IInterpolatable>
        => count.Fractions.Map(t => a.Lerp(b, t));

    // `count` evenly spaced values from a (inclusive) to b (exclusive); the
    // periodic form. Precondition: count >= 1.
    LinearSpaceExclusive(a: IInterpolatable, b: IInterpolatable, count: Integer): Array<IInterpolatable>
        => count.FractionsExclusive.Map(t => a.Lerp(b, t));

    // The sum of an array of numbers. The one numeric reduction the vocabulary
    // spells by name; the collection surface has no `Sum`.
    SumOf(values: Array<Number>): Number
        => values.Reduce(0.0, (acc, x) => acc + x);
}
```
